draft.title: How narratives shape values
card: A value is a belief about what is good, right or worth admiring. Stories often show values through what happens to characters.
Reward and punishment
A story can reward a behaviour, such as honesty, by giving a character a happy ending. It can punish a behaviour, such as greed, by letting it lead to loss or ruin.
Admire or judge
A writer can invite readers to admire a character, through a kind tone, or to judge one, through a mocking tone. Readers can still resist these invitations.
Over time
When many stories repeat the same patterns, they can help shape what a community sees as normal or right.
draft.remember: Stories show which behaviours win and which fail, and repeated patterns can shape a community's sense of right.

a.q: In a short story, Tariq lies to win a prize. His lie is exposed and he loses all his friends. What value does the story most likely promote?
opts: Honesty matters more than winning
Winning is worth any cost
Friends are not very important
Prizes should not be given
a.why: The lie is punished with the loss of his friends, so the story shows dishonesty failing. This invites readers to value honesty. The second option reverses this, because the story does not reward winning by lying.
a.clue: Look at what happens to Tariq after he lies.

b.q: Many films end with the lone hero beating a team of rivals and being cheered by the town. How might this repeated pattern shape a community's values over time?
opts: It may lead people to see individual success as admirable
It forces people to give up working in teams
It proves that rivals are always dishonest
It makes people stop watching films about teams
b.why: A repeated pattern of rewarding the lone hero can help make individual success seem normal and admirable. The second option is too strong: the card says stories can shape values, not that they force people to act.
b.clue: Think about what is rewarded each time, and the word can in the card.

b.best: It may lead people to see individual success as admirable

problems.detail: Why (a) names the 'second option' as the one that reverses the story's message, but the options are shuffled. The second option shown is 'Prizes should not be given', not 'Winning is worth any cost'. The why should name the option by its text.
Why (b) calls the 'forces' option the second option, but it appears first. The why should name the option by its text, not its position.

Every distractor uses absolute wording ('forces', 'proves', 'always', 'makes people stop'). The correct answer is the only hedged option ('may'), and the clue says to look for 'can'. Students can pick the answer from the wording alone without understanding the idea.
Question a is very easy for Year 11 Advanced. The value follows obviously from the outcome, and the distractors are implausible.

a.q: In a story, Ana ignores her coach's order to keep running and stops to help an injured rival. She loses the race, but the story ends with the crowd cheering her. What value does the story most likely promote?
opts: Helping others matters more than winning
Winning a race is what earns respect
Disobeying a coach is always the right choice
Losing a race leads to unhappiness
a.why: The behaviour the story rewards is Ana's choice to help, since the cheering comes after she stops for her rival. The option about disobeying a coach is tempting, but the story rewards her kindness, not disobedience in general.
a.clue: Ask which of Ana's choices the cheering rewards.

b.q: Many films end with a lone hero beating a team of rivals and being cheered by the town. How might this repeated pattern shape a community's values over time?
opts: It may make acting alone seem more admirable than teamwork
It may make teamwork seem more admirable than acting alone
It may have no effect, as each film is seen on its own
It may make the town's cheering seem foolish to viewers
b.why: Each film rewards the lone hero with cheering, and repeating that pattern can make acting alone seem normal and admirable. The option saying teamwork seems more admirable reverses this, because the team is the side that loses each time.
b.clue: Which behaviour gets the cheering in every film?

a.best: Helping others matters more than winning

b.best: It may make acting alone seem more admirable than teamwork
